The mandocello is a plucked instrument, the bass of the mandolin family, with a composite sounding classification, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-6. It is larger than the mandolin, its eight strings in four pairs each tuned in unison and the whole set in fifths from C2. The body may have a bowl back or a flat arched back, and the neck is longer. It sounds by plucking and is common in mandolin orchestras, quartets and Italian folk music, and also turns up occasionally in classical solo and modern folk music.
曼陀大提琴源自歐洲，與曼陀林家族同由義大利魯特琴系發展而來。巴洛克時期合奏興起，: The mandocello comes from Europe, developing with the mandolin family out of the Italian lute line. As ensemble playing grew in the Baroque period, the Vinaccia family of Naples promoted the metal-strung mandolin, and the mandalone may have been its predecessor. After the Paris exhibition of 1878 Italian players toured Europe and America, mandolin orchestras spread everywhere, and the mandocello took the bass part. Gibson made arched-back models from 1905 into the 1920s, Raffaele Calace wrote a tutor and advanced the design, and Luigi Embergher also improved it; after the 1930s the ensemble boom receded again.
曼陀大提琴為撥弦樂器，屬曼陀林家族的低音聲部，八弦成四對同度調音，整體按五度自低: The mandocello is a plucked instrument, the bass of the mandolin family, with eight strings in four pairs tuned in unison and the whole set in fifths from C2. The longer strings and low tuning give a range of about three and a half octaves, from two octaves below middle C to D#5/Eb5 or A5 depending on the number of frets, and the ten-string type reaches E6. Its low register is less bright and carrying than the mandolin's or the mandola's, and in a mandolin ensemble it can take both melody and bass. The bottom C string is thicker and may rattle when played loudly, so players may drop a string, change to a thinner one, or use amplification.
